pos: n. (two men: the father of Solomon's officer over the tribute, and a Levite of the return)
etymology: Hebrew Abda, servant, or servant of God, a shortened form built on ebed, a servant; borne by two men, 1 Kings 4:6 and Nehemiah 11:17.
biblical_def: Abda is the name of two men separated by four centuries, and in both cases the name — servant — is the whole of what Scripture tells us about the office. The first is named only as a father: “And Ahishar was over the household: and Adoniram the son of Abda was over the tribute” (1 Kings 4:6). His son held the hardest post in Solomon's cabinet, the levy of forced labour, and the Chronicler of Kings thought the father's name worth preserving beside it. The second Abda belongs to the restored city, and stands in a line of singers: “and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun” (Nehemiah 11:17). That genealogy reaches back to one of David's three chief musicians, so the second Abda is a servant in the oldest sense the word carries in Scripture: a man set apart to lead the thanksgiving of God's people. Nehemiah tells us why the office mattered to the returned remnant: “For in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God” (Nehemiah 12:46). Neither man says a word in Scripture. Both are named, and the naming is the point: the LORD keeps the roll of His servants whether or not the record keeps their words.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Abda, servant, or servant of God; the father of Adoniram who was over Solomon's tribute, and a Levite of the line of Jeduthun after the return.

corruption_summary: Service is now measured by visibility, so a name preserved without a deed attached looks to the modern reader like an empty entry rather than an honoured one.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to read a bare name in a register as filler — the part of Scripture one skips — because we have been trained to value the record only where it narrates achievement. Abda achieved nothing the text reports. He fathered a son who collected the levy, or he sang in the courts of the house of the LORD, and then the page turns. But the name means servant, and a servant's whole dignity is that he belongs to his master, not that he is remembered for his own work. To skip the registers is to miss how Scripture actually honours men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of being named by God: “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name” (Psalm 100:4). The second Abda stood in those gates, in a line four generations deep, doing what Jeduthun's house had been appointed to do. That is a life well spent, and the register is its monument.

pos: n. (a man of the house of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Abishur, father of the wall, or my father is a wall, from ab, father, and shur, a wall; named twice, 1 Chronicles 2:28-29.
biblical_def: Abishur stands in the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah, and his name is a confession: my father is a wall. He is introduced as a grandson: “And the sons of Onam were, Shammai, and Jada. And the sons of Shammai; Nadab, and Abishur” (1 Chronicles 2:28). The next verse gives him a wife and two sons, which in these registers is a mark of a house that continued: “And the name of the wife of Abishur was Abihail, and she bare him Ahban, and Molid” (1 Chronicles 2:29). The line runs from Hezron through Jerahmeel — “And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah” (1 Chronicles 2:25) — the collateral stock of Judah, not the royal line of David, and the Chronicler records it with the same care. Abihail is named, which is rarer in these lists than the men are; so is the fact that she bare him two sons. The house of a man whose name declares his father a wall is itself walled and continued. Scripture gives him no act, no office, and no word, only a wife and children, and that is the ordinary shape of covenant faithfulness in the generations between the great names.

corruption_summary: A genealogy that names a wife and the children she bore is read today as the record of a transaction, where Scripture presents it as the record of a household kept.
corruption_paragraphs: Progressive readings of the Hebrew registers treat a named wife as an exception that proves the rule of erasure, and an unnamed one as evidence of contempt. Neither reading attends to what the text does. Abihail is named because the Chronicler is tracing a house, and a house in Scripture is a man and a woman and the children given to them. The verse does not say Abishur acquired her; it says she bare him Ahban and Molid, which is the language of fruitfulness and gift, not of property.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that children are reckoned a reward and not a burden: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psalm 127:3). Abishur's name confessed that his father was a wall to him; his sons could say the same of him. That is how the covenant travels — household by household, wall by wall, through men the narrative never pauses on.

pos: n. (a Benjamite whose sons are reckoned in the Chronicler's register)
etymology: Hebrew Acher, another, or one following after, from the root meaning to be behind or to follow; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:12.
biblical_def: Aher is named once, at the close of a crowded Benjamite paragraph: “Shuppim also, and Huppim, the children of Ir, and Hushim, the sons of Aher” (1 Chronicles 7:12). His name means another, and the Authorized Version's own margin notes that some read it as Ahiram — the Benjamite head whose family is counted in the wilderness census: “of Ahiram, the family of the Ahiramites” (Numbers 26:38). The dictionary keeps the name the text prints. Benjamin's sons are listed thrice in Scripture and never in quite the same words, because the tribe was nearly destroyed in the days of the judges and rebuilt from a remnant; the earliest list runs “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21). Against that history, a head of a house called another is no small thing: the tribe went on having sons. Centuries later the apostle still named the stock he came from, “of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews” (Philippians 3:5). Aher is one of the quiet links by which that tribe survived to give Paul to the church.

corruption_summary: Where the Benjamite lists differ in spelling and order, critical reading treats the variation as proof of competing sources rather than of a tribe rebuilt from a remnant.
corruption_paragraphs: The three registers of Benjamin's sons — in Genesis, in Numbers, and in Chronicles — do not match name for name, and the standard academic move is to assign each to a different hand and a different century, so that the differences become evidence against the text rather than evidence about the tribe. Scripture itself supplies the better explanation. Benjamin was cut down to six hundred men in the matter of Gibeah and had to be rebuilt; a tribe reconstituted from a remnant will produce registers that differ in which houses survived to be counted, and the Authorized Version's margin is doing honest work when it records a second reading rather than hiding it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the preserving mercy of God toward a tribe that had earned destruction. Aher means another, and the plain fact that another Benjamite house could be named at all is the mercy. The remnant principle runs from Gibeah to Paul, who could still say what tribe he was of, and through him to the Gentiles. God does not need a large remnant; He needs a faithful one.

pos: n. (two men: a chief of the house of their fathers in Gad, and a son of Shamer in Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Achi, my brother, from ach, a brother; borne by two men, 1 Chronicles 5:15 and 7:34.
biblical_def: Ahi means my brother, and it is given to two men in the Chronicler's tribal registers. The first is a chief east of Jordan: “Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 5:15). The office is the point. A chief of the house of their fathers was the head of a kindred, answerable for its mustering and its inheritance, and the tribes beyond Jordan needed such men because they held exposed ground: “And they dwelt in Gilead in Bashan, and in her towns, and in all the suburbs of Sharon, upon their borders” (1 Chronicles 5:16). The same chapter counts what those borders cost — “of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skilful in war, were four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore, that went out to the war” (1 Chronicles 5:18). The second Ahi is in the far north, among Asher's sons: “And the sons of Shamer; Ahi, and Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram” (1 Chronicles 7:34). Two men on two frontiers, both called my brother: the name says what held Israel together when geography pulled it apart.

corruption_summary: Brotherhood is treated as sentiment today; in the tribal registers it was an office with a muster roll, a border to hold, and an inheritance to answer for.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic usage has reduced brotherhood to a feeling of belonging, so that a name meaning my brother reads as warmth and nothing more. The Chronicler's usage is harder and better. Ahi is named in the same breath as his office, chief of the house of their fathers, and two verses later the register counts the fighting men of those houses. Brotherhood here means a man is answerable for his kindred's land, its arms, and its place in Israel. It is a duty with a number attached to it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the tribes beyond Jordan were not a lesser Israel. They lived on the borders, they went out to the war, and their heads of houses were written into the same book as Judah's. A church that keeps only its central names loses what Chronicles is for: the whole people, named, including the ones holding the exposed ground.

pos: n. (a son of Shemida, of the tribe of Manasseh)
etymology: Hebrew Achyan, brotherly, or little brother, from ach, a brother; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:19.
biblical_def: Ahian is named once, in the Manassite register: “And the sons of Shemida were, Ahian, and Shechem, and Likhi, and Aniam” (1 Chronicles 7:19). His father Shemida heads one of the six families of Manasseh counted in the wilderness — “And of Shemida, the family of the Shemidaites: and of Hepher, the family of the Hepherites” (Numbers 26:32) — and the same six are the units by which Manasseh received its land: “for the children of Abiezer, and for the children of Helek, and for the children of Asriel, and for the children of Shechem, and for the children of Hepher, and for the children of Shemida: these were the male children of Manasseh the son of Joseph by their families” (Joshua 17:2). So Ahian is a son of one of the six, which means his name sits exactly where an inheritance was reckoned. The Chronicler is not padding. He is showing a people, generations after the conquest and after the exile, that the allotment of the land was made to named households and that those households had sons. The name itself — brotherly — belongs to a tribe that had to share a double portion with its brother Ephraim and live beside it.

corruption_summary: The land allotments are read as a tribal origin myth projected backward; Scripture presents them as a deed register naming the households that actually received ground.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatment of Joshua and Chronicles commonly dates the allotment lists late and reads them as a retrojection written to justify later landholding. The documents themselves behave differently. They name six Manassite families in the wilderness, name the same six at the division of the land, and then name the sons within one of them centuries later. That is the behaviour of a kept register, not of a founding legend. A legend grows names; a register keeps them, and keeps the awkward ones.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the inheritance was given by name and by household. Manasseh's portion was not a vague claim to territory but a lot measured out to the children of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. Ahian is a son in the last of those houses. God deals with families, and He writes down which ones.

pos: n. (a Kohathite Levite, son of Elkanah)
etymology: Hebrew Achimoth, brother of death, from ach, a brother, and maveth, death; named once, 1 Chronicles 6:25.
biblical_def: Ahimoth appears in a single clause of the Levitical register: “And the sons of Elkanah; Amasai, and Ahimoth” (1 Chronicles 6:25). The name is startling — brother of death — and it is given to a man in the one tribe appointed to handle holy things, where death was a standing hazard rather than a figure of speech. He is a Kohathite, of the clan that carried the ark and the vessels of the sanctuary; Kohath's own sons are named in the law: “And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel: and the years of the life of Kohath were an hundred thirty and three years” (Exodus 6:18). The same chapter of Chronicles shows what the house became: “Of the sons of the Kohathites: Heman a singer, the son of Joel, the son of Shemuel” (1 Chronicles 6:33), and describes the work they did before the temple stood — “And they ministered before the dwelling place of the tabernacle of the congregation with singing, until Solomon had built the house of the LORD in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 6:32). A man named for death stands in the ancestry of the men who sang. That is the Levitical story in miniature.

corruption_summary: A name carrying death is softened or explained away, when Scripture gives it plainly to a man of the tribe that bore holy things at peril of life.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern naming sentiment cannot easily receive a name like brother of death, and reference works often reach for an alternate etymology to spare the reader. The Authorized Version does not soften it, and neither should a dictionary. The Levites handled what killed the unauthorised; Uzzah died for touching the ark, and the sons of Aaron died for strange fire. A Kohathite house in which a man is called the brother of death is a house that knew what its office was.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that holiness is dangerous before it is comforting, and that the ministry of praise grew out of a ministry conducted under threat of death. Ahimoth's line ends in Heman, who sang before the dwelling place of the tabernacle. The songs of Israel came from men who had every reason to fear the God they sang to, which is why the songs are worth singing.

pos: n. (a Benjamite, son of Bilhan, of the house of Jediael)
etymology: Hebrew Achishachar, brother of the dawn, from ach, a brother, and shachar, the dawn or morning; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:10.
biblical_def: Ahishahar closes a list of seven brothers: “The sons also of Jediael; Bilhan: and the sons of Bilhan; Jeush, and Benjamin, and Ehud, and Chenaanah, and Zethan, and Tharshish, and Ahishahar” (1 Chronicles 7:10). His name means brother of the dawn, and the verse that follows tells the reader what these seven houses amounted to: “All these the sons of Jediael, by the heads of their fathers, mighty men of valour, were seventeen thousand and two hundred soldiers, fit to go out for war and battle” (1 Chronicles 7:11). Jediael is one of the three Benjamite heads the Chronicler names — “The sons of Benjamin; Bela, and Becher, and Jediael, three” (1 Chronicles 7:6) — so Ahishahar is a head of a house within a fighting tribe. Benjamin's men were known for a particular skill: “They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 12:2). A man called brother of the dawn in a tribe of archers is a reminder that the day breaks for soldiers too, and that the LORD numbers the houses that go out to battle.

corruption_summary: Military census is read as glorification of violence, where Scripture reckons the fighting strength of named households as a sober fact of life in a fallen world.
corruption_paragraphs: A register that counts seventeen thousand two hundred soldiers offends the modern conscience, which prefers Scripture to be about interior experience and reads a muster roll as militarism. But the Chronicler is not celebrating slaughter; he is telling a returned and defenceless remnant what their fathers' houses had once been able to field. The honest reading does not flinch at the number and does not glory in it either. Israel lived among enemies, and the heads of houses were answerable for the men who went out.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that strength is to be numbered honestly and never trusted. The same book that counts Jediael's seventeen thousand records what came of trusting such numbers. A man named brother of the dawn in such a list points past the muster: the morning belongs to God, who gives and withholds victory, and the soldier who sees the dawn sees a mercy he did not count.

pos: n. (a son of Ashur the father of Tekoa, of the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Achuzzam, their possession, or possessor, from achaz, to take hold, to seize; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:6.
biblical_def: Ahuzam is the first-named son of a second wife: “And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:6). The household is set out a verse earlier: “And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:5). His name means their possession — the root is the verb to take hold — and he stands in the Judah chapter that runs from Hezron's descendants down to the craftsmen and the men of Tekoa. Four verses later the same chapter gives the prayer it is best known for: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Ahuzam and Jabez stand within a few lines of each other, and the juxtaposition is instructive: one man is named possession, and the next man asks God to enlarge his. The register is not inert; it is the setting in which that prayer is answered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Ahuzam, their possession, or possessor; a son of Ashur the father of Tekoa by his wife Naarah, of the tribe of Judah.
webster_full: Hebrew Achuzzam, their possession, or possessor.
From achaz, to take hold, to seize, to hold fast.
It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at 1 Chronicles 4:6.
He was a son of Ashur the father of Tekoa, by his wife Naarah.
His name stands in the chapter of Judah that also records the prayer of Jabez.
scriptures: And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.
And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.

And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
corruption_summary: Possession is heard now as acquisition and grievance; the name means a child received as a holding from God, not an estate seized from a neighbour.
corruption_paragraphs: The vocabulary of possession has been captured by a politics in which to hold anything is to have taken it from someone, so a man named their possession reads as an indictment. The Hebrew sense is otherwise. An achuzzah is a holding received and held fast — the word used of the land God gave Israel and of the burying place Abraham bought. Applied to a child it means a son reckoned as the family's treasure, which is precisely how Scripture elsewhere speaks of children.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that what God gives is held, not grasped: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psalm 127:3). Four verses from Ahuzam's name, Jabez asks God to enlarge his coast and is answered. The chapter teaches the right posture toward every holding — ask for it, receive it from His hand, and hold it as a trust.

pos: n. (a man of the house of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Appayim, the nostrils, or the face, the dual of aph, a nostril; named twice, 1 Chronicles 2:30-31.
biblical_def: Appaim is named with his brother and with his brother's childlessness: “And the sons of Nadab; Seled, and Appaim: but Seled died without children” (1 Chronicles 2:30). The register then follows Appaim's line for three generations and halts: “And the sons of Appaim; Ishi. And the sons of Ishi; Sheshan. And the children of Sheshan; Ahlai” (1 Chronicles 2:31). That thinning line is the subject of the next verses, which record an extraordinary measure: “Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha” (1 Chronicles 2:34), and Sheshan gave his daughter to that servant so the house would not die out. Appaim's branch of Jerahmeel — “And the sons of Jonathan; Peleth, and Zaza. These were the sons of Jerahmeel” (1 Chronicles 2:33) — is therefore the Chronicler's case study in a house preserved by one thread. His name means the nostrils, the Hebrew seat of breath and of anger; and Scripture lets the reader watch a family that very nearly stopped breathing continue anyway.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Appaim, the nostrils, or the face; a son of Nadab of the house of Jerahmeel, whose line narrowed to a single heir.
webster_full: Hebrew Appayim, the nostrils, or the face.
The dual of aph, a nostril; the Hebrew seat of breath and of anger.
It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, at 1 Chronicles 2:30 and 2:31.
He was a son of Nadab, of the house of Jerahmeel in Judah.
His line ran through Ishi and Sheshan to Ahlai, and was preserved through a daughter.
scriptures: And the sons of Nadab; Seled, and Appaim: but Seled died without children.
And the sons of Appaim; Ishi. And the sons of Ishi; Sheshan. And the children of Sheshan; Ahlai.
Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha.
And the sons of Jonathan; Peleth, and Zaza. These were the sons of Jerahmeel.
corruption_summary: A childless death and a line narrowed to one heir are read as misfortune and nothing more, where Chronicles treats them as the ordinary way God preserves a remnant.
corruption_paragraphs: The register says bluntly that Seled died without children, and the modern habit is either to pass over such a clause or to read it as a judgment on the man. Chronicles is doing something else. It is showing how narrow the channel was through which the house of Jerahmeel passed, and then showing the measure taken to keep it open. Nothing in the text treats childlessness as a verdict on anyone's standing before God; it treats it as a fact that makes the surviving line precious.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the thinness of the thread by which covenant lines are kept, and the LORD's habit of keeping them. Appaim's branch came down to a man with no sons, and continued through a daughter and a servant from Egypt. The genealogies of Scripture are full of such narrow places, and they all run toward the one line that mattered.

pos: n. (three men: a chief in Manasseh, a ruler of Naphtali under David, and the father of Jeremiah's pursuer)
etymology: Hebrew Azriel, help of God, or God is my help, from azar, to help, and El, God; borne by three men, 1 Chronicles 5:24, 27:19, Jeremiah 36:26.
biblical_def: Azriel means God is my help, and it is given to three men whose circumstances differ sharply. The first is a tribal chief east of Jordan: “And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 5:24). The second is remembered through his son in David's administration: “of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel” (1 Chronicles 27:19). The third stands on the wrong side of a famous scene. When Jehoiakim had burned the scroll, “the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them” (Jeremiah 36:26). The princes had already warned the two men — “Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be” (Jeremiah 36:19) — and the name of the man sent to arrest the prophet is the son of one called help of God. The irony is the text's own, and the help went to the hunted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Azriel, help of God, or God is my help; borne by a Manassite chief, by the father of David's ruler over Naphtali, and by the father of one sent to seize Jeremiah.
webster_full: Hebrew Azriel, help of God, or God is my help.
From azar, to help or succour, with El, God.
It occurs three times in the Authorized Version: 1 Chronicles 5:24, 1 Chronicles 27:19, and Jeremiah 36:26.
The first was a head of a father's house among the tribes east of Jordan.
The third was father of Seraiah, whom Jehoiakim sent to take Baruch and Jeremiah.
scriptures: And these were the heads of the house of their fathers, even Epher, and Ishi, and Eliel, and Azriel, and Jeremiah, and Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of the house of their fathers.
Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel:
But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them.
Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be.
corruption_summary: Divine help is reduced to a feeling of support; the name is attached in Scripture to men on both sides of a persecution, and the help proves to be God's own hiding of His prophet.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic religion treats help from God as inward reassurance, so a name meaning God is my help is heard as a sentiment about how the bearer felt. Jeremiah 36 refuses that reading. The help in question is concrete and external: a king issues an arrest warrant, officers go out, and “the LORD hid them”. Divine help there is an act in history with a result you could verify by looking for two men and failing to find them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a godly name is no guarantee of a godly house, and no obstacle to God's purpose. Seraiah son of Azriel carried a warrant against the word of God; the scroll he was sent to suppress was rewritten with more added to it. The preservation of Scripture does not depend on the goodwill of the men who handle it, and the help named in Azriel belonged, that day, to the prophet and not to the officer.
